- The information systems are built as pure rules first, in parallel with the online work. `objectives-endgame` wires them in.
- There are nine named sectors (3 × 3), computed from the map size, so the same code serves the slice sea and the 12-island alpha.
- Rumors never name ids or exact positions. They prefer sealed sources, then caches, then a carrier sighting. Carrier sightings come from a snapshot 30–60 s old (never current), which helps a player choose a route without giving them a tracker (§11).
- The module reads a caller-built world view instead of importing the ledger, the same decoupling as the claim code.
- The only exact position ever sent is the final island's, and only to a player holding a full set (§5).

- Corrected after design challenge attempt 1 (its alternative, adopted): carrier sightings are one-shot and never go stale, at most one per player per 30 s before minute 28, so a victim can't track the thief. Only island and cache rumors go stale. Broadcasts carry a sector and a type, never a player. Losses come from diffing held types. Reveals fire on crossing boundaries.

- Corrected after design challenge attempt 2: stale means emptied by collection (theft can't empty an island or a cache); targeted rumors carry a request id and get an outcome, so gold is charged only when something is delivered and retries can't double-spend (§11); carrier data comes from two 30 s snapshots, so a sighting is 30–60 s old, a deliberate small relaxation of "exactly 30 s"; capped free sightings are deferred, never dropped; duel-reserved rubbings still count as held.

## Assumptions

- The final island's position and the control start tick come from the config (the final-island sockets arrive with `objectives-endgame`).
- The slice uses two rubbing types, so "all types" means both, per the preset.

## Deferred

- Wiring, the journal UI, buying rumors and dockside shops: `objectives-endgame`.

Build the match's information systems as pure, deterministic rules. They tell a player where to go and when the race tightens:

- coarse, delayed carrier sightings;
- the sea sectors;

This information is what turns exploring into a race and brings players into conflict, so it must be useful but never a free tracker. Every output is addressed to specific players (§16). `objectives-endgame` wires it into the match room later. This feature only builds and proves the rules.

## Context

- Independent of the ledger's code: the caller passes a per-tick **world view** (for each rubbing, its type and where it is: a sealed source with its island, a cache position, a carrier with position, or reserved in a duel; each player's held types and position; which islands are claimed out). Don't import `objectives`, so the two stay decoupled. Gold for bought rumors is the caller's (ledger) business; this module only generates the rumor.
- Pure and integer: no Phaser, Colyseus, DOM, timers, wall-clock time, `Math.random` or floating-point transcendental functions. Time is the world tick (20 per second). Randomness comes from the seeded generator (`random.ts`). Durations are named content constants in seconds, converted to ticks.

7	+# Match information (intel)
8	+
9	+The pure rules behind §2's timed reveals, §3's rumors and journal, §5's final-island announcement and §11's comeback leads. `@pirate-sea-race/simulation/intel` has the config, the state, `stepIntel`, `targetedRumorAvailability` and `replayIntel`. `@pirate-sea-race/content/intel` has the constants and the zod validator `validateIntelRules`. The module doesn't import the ledger. It is integer data with no clocks and no `Math.random`, and time is the world tick (20 per second). `objectives-endgame` wires it into `MatchRoom`; nothing calls it yet.
10	+
11	+## Constants (`intelRules`)
12	+
13	+| Rule | Value |
14	+| --- | --- |
15	+| Sector grid | 3 × 3, named row by row from "North-West Reach" to "South-East Reach" |
16	+| Sighting delay | 600 ticks (30 s), equal to the carrier interval |
17	+| Carrier interval | 600 ticks (30 s) |
18	+| Sector reveal | 24,000 ticks (minute 20) after control start |
19	+| Carrier reveal | 33,600 ticks (minute 28) after control start |
20	+| Targeted rumor price | 25 gold (the caller charges it) |
21	+
22	+The validator refuses a zero interval, reveals out of order, a delay that differs from the interval, and names that are missing or repeated.
23	+
24	+## Sectors
25	+
26	+`sectorOfTile` cuts the map's columns and rows into three bands each by integer division (`floor(tile × 3 / width)`). Every tile is in exactly one sector, and bands differ by at most one tile. On the 224 × 208 slice sea, the columns start at tiles 0, 75 and 150 and the rows at 0, 70 and 139. `sectorOf(position)` is the sector of the position's tile. A position off the map counts in the nearest edge sector. The config computes all of this from the map size, so the same code serves the slice and the 12-island alpha.
27	+
28	+## Leads
29	+
30	+A rumor names a missing type and a target: an **island**, where a source of that type is still sealed, or a **sector**, where a recovery cache holds one. It never names a rubbing, a player or a position. The generator picks among the eligible targets with the seeded generator (`random.ts`), so the same seed gives the same rumor. It tries three tiers in order:
31	+
32	+1. the islands with a sealed source of the type;
33	+2. the sectors with a cached copy;
34	+3. a **carrier sighting**, and only when every copy of the type is carried by someone else.
35	+
36	+Targets already active in the player's journal are skipped, so a player is never given the same lead twice.
37	+
38	+Leads are made on four occasions:
39	+
40	+- a **start** rumor for each player at control start, or when a player is first seen after it;
41	+- a free **fresh** rumor for each type a player lost (§11);
42	+- a **targeted** rumor, bought on request;
43	+- a **replacement**, when a journal rumor goes stale.
44	+
45	+Losses and completions come from diffing each player's held types between ticks. A rubbing reserved in a duel still counts as held, so entering a duel is never a loss; only a settled theft is.
46	+
47	+**Journal rumors** (island or sector) are the only leads tracked:
48	+
49	+- A rumor goes **stale** when its target no longer holds its type: the source was collected or the cache claimed by someone else. The player gets `rumor-stale` with the tick and then a replacement.
50	+- A rumor whose type the holder obtains, by any means, is **resolved** quietly. It gets no replacement.
51	+
52	+**Carrier sightings** are one-shot messages, never tracked, so they can never go stale and can't be used to follow a carrier. At every carrier boundary (control start plus a multiple of 30 s, counted when crossed), the state takes one snapshot of the carried copies: the sector, the type and the internal holder of each. It keeps the latest two. A sighting reads the **older** of the two, so it is 30–60 s old and never the current position. It also skips the requester's own former entries.
53	+
54	+Before minute 28, a player gets at most one sighting per snapshot. A targeted request that hits this cap is answered `capped`. A free trigger (start, fresh or replacement) that hits the cap, or that finds no usable snapshot yet, is **deferred**: it is retried at each later boundary until it is delivered, turns into a journal rumor because a source or cache has become available, or becomes moot because the player obtained the type. A player has at most one pending sighting per type, and deliveries still respect the cap. A free trigger with nothing at all to point at sends `no-lead`.
55	+
56	+**Targeted requests** are `{ requestId, playerId, type }`, and each gets exactly one outcome, whatever the order of the batch:
57	+
58	+- `rumor` or `sighting`: something was delivered. Charge the 25 gold only for these two.
59	+- `capped`: the player already got a sighting in this snapshot.
60	+- `none`: nothing to sell. The player holds the type, or the player is unknown, or it is before control start, or no untracked target exists.
61	+- `duplicate`: the request id was seen before. The step answers it without changing the state or drawing from the generator.
62	+
63	+`targetedRumorAvailability(config, state, view, playerId, type)` gives the same answer without drawing, so the UI can show whether buying would yield anything.
64	+
65	+## Reveals (§2, §5)
66	+
67	+All reveals fire when their tick is crossed since the last processed tick, so a skipped tick never loses one. Nothing is sent before control start.
68	+
69	+- **First full set:** the first player to hold every type of the preset triggers `final-sector` (the final island's sector) to everyone. Each holder of a full set gets `final-route` with the exact point: the first completer, later completers, and anyone who restores a broken set (with `restored: true`). A player who loses a type gets `final-route-inactive`.
70	+- **Minute 20:** `sector-reveal` to everyone, listing the sectors with sealed sources and the sectors with caches.
71	+- **Minute 28, then every 30 s:** `carrier-report` to everyone, listing the (sector, type) pairs of the newest snapshot. Skipping several beats sends one report.
72	+- **Minute 35** belongs to the claim code.
73	+
74	+## Messages and hidden information (§16)
75	+
76	+`stepIntel(config, state, view, requests) → { state, messages, outcomes }` never writes into its input. Each message is `{ to, body }`, where `to` is `{ kind: "player", playerId }`, `{ kind: "players", playerIds }` or `{ kind: "everyone" }`. Broadcasts are `final-sector`, `sector-reveal` and `carrier-report`; every other kind goes to one player.
77	+
78	+Bodies carry sectors, island indexes and names, types, ticks and journal entry numbers. They never carry a player id, a rubbing id, or a source's, cache's or ship's position. The one exact position ever sent is the final island's, in a `final-route` to a full-set holder. The property tests check every message of every run against these rules:
79	+
80	+- five seeded runs with compressed reveal times;
81	+- one slice run with the real constants for 36,660 ticks;
82	+- one alpha run with the real constants that skips ticks.
83	+
84	+Their `EXERCISED` check asserts that every message kind, outcome and lead path occurred.
85	+
86	+## Building the world view from the ledger
87	+
88	+On each processed tick, the caller passes `{ tick, players, rubbings }`:
89	+
90	+- **`players`:** each player still in the match (`status` not `left`), with the ship's position in sub-units.
91	+- **`rubbings`:** each ledger rubbing with its `type` and its `location` resolved to a place:
92	+  - `source` becomes `{ kind: "source", island, x, y }` from its `LedgerSource`;
93	+  - `cache` becomes `{ kind: "cache", x, y }` from its `LedgerCache`;
94	+  - `player` becomes `{ kind: "carried", playerId }`;
95	+  - `duel` becomes `{ kind: "duel", playerId }`.
96	+
97	+Held types and claimed-out islands (islands with no sealed source left) follow from the rubbings, so they can't disagree with them. The ledger's sticky `freshRumors` flag isn't read. The config comes from `createIntelConfig({ preset, finalIsland, controlStartTick, map })`. The state comes from `createIntelState(config, seed)`, which starts before control start.
98	+
99	+## Decisions taken here
100	+
101	+- Held types and claimed-out islands are derived from the view's rubbings rather than passed separately.
102	+- A pending sighting is kept per type, so two types that need a sighting at once are both delivered, one per snapshot, rather than one being dropped.
103	+- A free trigger that finds every copy carried but no snapshot entry to read yet waits like a capped one.
104	+- Targeted requests in one batch are handled in request-id order, so the order they are listed in never changes the result.

+# Match information (intel)
+
+The pure rules behind §2's timed reveals, §3's rumors and journal, §5's final-island announcement and §11's comeback leads. `@pirate-sea-race/simulation/intel` has the config, the state, `stepIntel`, `targetedRumorAvailability` and `replayIntel`. `@pirate-sea-race/content/intel` has the constants and the zod validator `validateIntelRules`. The module doesn't import the ledger. It is integer data with no clocks and no `Math.random`, and time is the world tick (20 per second). `objectives-endgame` wires it into `MatchRoom`; nothing calls it yet.
+
+## Constants (`intelRules`)
+
+| Rule | Value |
+| --- | --- |
+| Sector grid | 3 × 3, named row by row from "North-West Reach" to "South-East Reach" |
+| Sighting delay | 600 ticks (30 s), equal to the carrier interval |
+| Carrier interval | 600 ticks (30 s) |
+| Sector reveal | 24,000 ticks (minute 20) after control start |
+| Carrier reveal | 33,600 ticks (minute 28) after control start |
+| Targeted rumor price | 25 gold (the caller charges it) |
+
+The validator refuses a zero interval, reveals out of order, a delay that differs from the interval, and names that are missing or repeated.
+
+## Sectors
+
+`sectorOfTile` cuts the map's columns and rows into three bands each by integer division (`floor(tile × 3 / width)`). Every tile is in exactly one sector, and bands differ by at most one tile. On the 224 × 208 slice sea, the columns start at tiles 0, 75 and 150 and the rows at 0, 70 and 139. `sectorOf(position)` is the sector of the position's tile. A position off the map counts in the nearest edge sector. The config computes all of this from the map size, so the same code serves the slice and the 12-island alpha.
+
+## Leads
+
+A rumor names a missing type and a target: an **island**, where a source of that type is still sealed, or a **sector**, where a recovery cache holds one. It never names a rubbing, a player or a position. The generator picks among the eligible targets with the seeded generator (`random.ts`), so the same seed gives the same rumor. It tries three tiers in order:
+
+1. the islands with a sealed source of the type;
+2. the sectors with a cached copy;
+3. a **carrier sighting**, and only when every copy of the type is carried by someone else.
+
+Targets already active in the player's journal are skipped, so a player is never given the same lead twice.
+
+Leads are made on four occasions:
+
+- a **start** rumor for each player at control start, or when a player is first seen after it;
+- a free **fresh** rumor for each type a player lost (§11);
+- a **targeted** rumor, bought on request;
+- a **replacement**, when a journal rumor goes stale.
+
+Losses and completions come from diffing each player's held types between ticks. A rubbing reserved in a duel still counts as held, so entering a duel is never a loss; only a settled theft is.
+
+**Journal rumors** (island or sector) are the only leads tracked:
+
+- A rumor goes **stale** when its target no longer holds its type: the source was collected or the cache claimed by someone else. The player gets `rumor-stale` with the tick and then a replacement.
+- A rumor whose type the holder obtains, by any means, is **resolved** quietly. It gets no replacement.
+
+**Carrier sightings** are one-shot messages, never tracked, so they can never go stale and can't be used to follow a carrier. At every carrier boundary (control start plus a multiple of 30 s, counted when crossed), the state takes one snapshot of the carried copies: the sector, the type and the internal holder of each. It keeps the latest two. A sighting reads the **older** of the two, so it is 30–60 s old and never the current position. It also skips the requester's own former entries.
+
+Before minute 28, a player gets at most one sighting per snapshot. A targeted request that hits this cap is answered `capped`. A free trigger (start, fresh or replacement) that hits the cap, or that finds no usable snapshot yet, is **deferred**: it is retried at each later boundary until it is delivered, turns into a journal rumor because a source or cache has become available, or becomes moot because the player obtained the type. A player has at most one pending sighting per type, and deliveries still respect the cap. A free trigger with nothing at all to point at sends `no-lead`.
+
+**Targeted requests** are `{ requestId, playerId, type }`, and each gets exactly one outcome, whatever the order of the batch:
+
+- `rumor` or `sighting`: something was delivered. Charge the 25 gold only for these two.
+- `capped`: the player already got a sighting in this snapshot.
+- `none`: nothing to sell. The player holds the type, or the player is unknown, or it is before control start, or no untracked target exists.
+- `duplicate`: the request id was seen before. The step answers it without changing the state or drawing from the generator.
+
+`targetedRumorAvailability(config, state, view, playerId, type)` gives the same answer without drawing, so the UI can show whether buying would yield anything.
+
+## Reveals (§2, §5)
+
+All reveals fire when their tick is crossed since the last processed tick, so a skipped tick never loses one. Nothing is sent before control start.
+
+- **First full set:** the first player to hold every type of the preset triggers `final-sector` (the final island's sector) to everyone. Each holder of a full set gets `final-route` with the exact point: the first completer, later completers, and anyone who restores a broken set (with `restored: true`). A player who loses a type gets `final-route-inactive`.
+- **Minute 20:** `sector-reveal` to everyone, listing the sectors with sealed sources and the sectors with caches.
+- **Minute 28, then every 30 s:** `carrier-report` to everyone, listing the (sector, type) pairs of the newest snapshot. Skipping several beats sends one report.
+- **Minute 35** belongs to the claim code.
+
+## Messages and hidden information (§16)
+
+`stepIntel(config, state, view, requests) → { state, messages, outcomes }` never writes into its input. Each message is `{ to, body }`, where `to` is `{ kind: "player", playerId }`, `{ kind: "players", playerIds }` or `{ kind: "everyone" }`. Broadcasts are `final-sector`, `sector-reveal` and `carrier-report`; every other kind goes to one player.
+
+Bodies carry sectors, island indexes and names, types, ticks and journal entry numbers. They never carry a player id, a rubbing id, or a source's, cache's or ship's position. The one exact position ever sent is the final island's, in a `final-route` to a full-set holder. The property tests check every message of every run against these rules:
+
+- five seeded runs with compressed reveal times;
+- one slice run with the real constants for 36,660 ticks;
+- one alpha run with the real constants that skips ticks.
+
+Their `EXERCISED` check asserts that every message kind, outcome and lead path occurred.
+
+## Building the world view from the ledger
+
+On each processed tick, the caller passes `{ tick, players, rubbings }`:
+
+- **`players`:** each player still in the match (`status` not `left`), with the ship's position in sub-units.
+- **`rubbings`:** each ledger rubbing with its `type` and its `location` resolved to a place:
+  - `source` becomes `{ kind: "source", island, x, y }` from its `LedgerSource`;
+  - `cache` becomes `{ kind: "cache", x, y }` from its `LedgerCache`;
+  - `player` becomes `{ kind: "carried", playerId }`;
+  - `duel` becomes `{ kind: "duel", playerId }`.
+
+Held types and claimed-out islands (islands with no sealed source left) follow from the rubbings, so they can't disagree with them. The ledger's sticky `freshRumors` flag isn't read. The config comes from `createIntelConfig({ preset, finalIsland, controlStartTick, map })`. The state comes from `createIntelState(config, seed)`, which starts before control start.
+
+## Decisions taken here
+
+- Held types and claimed-out islands are derived from the view's rubbings rather than passed separately.
+- A pending sighting is kept per type, so two types that need a sighting at once are both delivered, one per snapshot, rather than one being dropped.
+- A free trigger that finds every copy carried but no snapshot entry to read yet waits like a capped one.
+- Targeted requests in one batch are handled in request-id order, so the order they are listed in never changes the result.

+import { z } from "zod";
+import { formatIssues, type ValidationResult } from "../rules.js";
+import { WORLD_STEPS_PER_SECOND } from "../sailing.js";
+
+/** The sea is split into a grid of named sectors this many columns wide and rows high (§2's "sectors"). */
+export const SECTOR_COLUMNS = 3;
+export const SECTOR_ROWS = 3;
+
+/** The nine sector names, row by row from the north-west corner. */
+export const SECTOR_NAMES = [
+  "North-West Reach",
+  "Northern Waters",
+  "North-East Reach",
+  "Western Waters",
+  "Central Waters",
+  "Eastern Waters",
+  "South-West Reach",
+  "Southern Waters",
+  "South-East Reach",
+] as const;
+
+/**
+ * §11: a carrier sighting is coarse and delayed. It reads the carrier snapshot taken one interval before the latest,
+ * so it is at least this old (and less than twice this old), never the current location.
+ */
+export const CARRIER_SIGHTING_DELAY_SECONDS = 30;
+/** §2: from minute 28 the carriers' sectors are published every 30 seconds; the carrier snapshots keep the same beat. */
+export const CARRIER_INTERVAL_SECONDS = 30;
+/** §2: at minute 20 the sectors holding unclaimed rubbings and abandoned caches are revealed. */
+export const SECTOR_REVEAL_MINUTE = 20;
+/** §2: from minute 28 the carriers' approximate sectors are published. */
+export const CARRIER_REVEAL_MINUTE = 28;
+/** §11: what the caller charges for a targeted rumor that delivers something. */
+export const TARGETED_RUMOR_GOLD = 25;
+
+/** The information rules (§2, §3, §11) in world ticks (20 a second), counted from the start of player control. */
+export const intelRulesSchema = z
+  .strictObject({
+    sectorColumns: z.int().positive(),
+    sectorRows: z.int().positive(),
+    /** Row by row from the north-west; one unique, non-empty name per sector. */
+    sectorNames: z.array(z.string().min(1)),
+    /** How old a carrier sighting is at least; it must equal the carrier interval, since sightings read the previous snapshot. */
+    sightingDelayTicks: z.int().positive(),
+    /** The beat of the carrier snapshots, of the sighting cap and, from the carrier reveal on, of the carrier broadcasts. */
+    carrierIntervalTicks: z.int().positive(),
+    /** Ticks from control start to the reveal of the sectors holding unclaimed rubbings and caches. */
+    sectorRevealTicks: z.int().positive(),
+    /** Ticks from control start to the first carrier broadcast. */
+    carrierRevealTicks: z.int().positive(),
+    targetedRumorGold: z.int().nonnegative(),
+  })
+  .superRefine((rules, ctx) => {
+    if (rules.sectorNames.length !== rules.sectorColumns * rules.sectorRows) {
+      ctx.addIssue({
+        code: "custom",
+        path: ["sectorNames"],
+        message: `${rules.sectorNames.length} names for a ${rules.sectorColumns} × ${rules.sectorRows} grid`,
+      });
+    }
+    if (new Set(rules.sectorNames).size !== rules.sectorNames.length) {
+      ctx.addIssue({ code: "custom", path: ["sectorNames"], message: "sector names must be unique" });
+    }
+    if (rules.sightingDelayTicks !== rules.carrierIntervalTicks) {
+      ctx.addIssue({
+        code: "custom",
+        path: ["sightingDelayTicks"],
+        message: `the sighting delay (${rules.sightingDelayTicks} ticks) must equal the carrier interval (${rules.carrierIntervalTicks} ticks)`,
+      });
+    }
+    if (rules.sectorRevealTicks >= rules.carrierRevealTicks) {
+      ctx.addIssue({
+        code: "custom",
+        path: ["carrierRevealTicks"],
+        message: `the carrier reveal (${rules.carrierRevealTicks} ticks) must come after the sector reveal (${rules.sectorRevealTicks} ticks)`,
+      });
+    }
+  });
+
+export type IntelRules = z.infer<typeof intelRulesSchema>;
+
+export const intelRules: IntelRules = {
+  sectorColumns: SECTOR_COLUMNS,
+  sectorRows: SECTOR_ROWS,
+  sectorNames: [...SECTOR_NAMES],
+  sightingDelayTicks: CARRIER_SIGHTING_DELAY_SECONDS * WORLD_STEPS_PER_SECOND,
+  carrierIntervalTicks: CARRIER_INTERVAL_SECONDS * WORLD_STEPS_PER_SECOND,
+  sectorRevealTicks: SECTOR_REVEAL_MINUTE * 60 * WORLD_STEPS_PER_SECOND,
+  carrierRevealTicks: CARRIER_REVEAL_MINUTE * 60 * WORLD_STEPS_PER_SECOND,
+  targetedRumorGold: TARGETED_RUMOR_GOLD,
+};
+
+export function validateIntelRules(candidate: unknown): ValidationResult<IntelRules> {
+  const parsed = intelRulesSchema.safeParse(candidate);
+  return parsed.success ? { ok: true, value: parsed.data } : { ok: false, issues: formatIssues(parsed.error) };
+}

+import { describe, expect, it } from "vitest";

+
+const T = 256;
+const tile = (x: number, y: number): IntelPoint => ({ x: x * T + 128, y: y * T + 128 });
+/** A 30 × 30 test sea: sector bands are tiles 0–9, 10–19 and 20–29. Islands sit in the four corner sectors. */

+const ISLAND_SECTOR = [0, 2, 6, 8];

+const S = [tile(2, 2), tile(15, 2), tile(27, 2), tile(2, 15), tile(15, 15), tile(27, 15), tile(2, 27), tile(15, 27), tile(27, 27)] as const;
+const FINAL = { x: 15 * T + 7, y: 16 * T + 3 };
+const START = 100;
+
+/** Real reveal times and a 100-tick (5 s) carrier interval, so carrier scenarios stay short. */
+const quick = createIntelConfig({
+  preset: "slice",
+  finalIsland: FINAL,
+  controlStartTick: START,
+  map: MAP,
+  rules: { ...intelRules, carrierIntervalTicks: 100, sightingDelayTicks: 100, sectorRevealTicks: 1_000, carrierRevealTicks: 2_000 },
+});
+const real = createIntelConfig({ preset: "slice", finalIsland: FINAL, controlStartTick: START, map: MAP });
+
+const typeOf = (id: string) => id.slice(0, id.indexOf("-")) as RubbingType;
+const source = (id: string, island: number): IntelRubbing => ({ id, type: typeOf(id), place: { kind: "source", island, ...ISLAND_AT[island]! } });
+const cached = (id: string, at: IntelPoint): IntelRubbing => ({ id, type: typeOf(id), place: { kind: "cache", ...at } });
+const carried = (id: string, playerId: string): IntelRubbing => ({ id, type: typeOf(id), place: { kind: "carried", playerId } });
+const reserved = (id: string, playerId: string): IntelRubbing => ({ id, type: typeOf(id), place: { kind: "duel", playerId } });
+
+interface World {
+  readonly players: Readonly<Record<string, IntelPoint>>;
+  readonly rubbings: readonly IntelRubbing[];
+}
+
+/** Recursively frozen, so a step that mutated its input would throw. */
+function deepFreeze<T>(value: T): T {
+  if (typeof value === "object" && value !== null && !Object.isFrozen(value)) {
+    Object.freeze(value);
+    for (const child of Object.values(value)) deepFreeze(child);
+  }
+  return value;
+}
+
+function viewOf(tick: number, world: World): IntelWorldView {
+  return { tick, players: Object.entries(world.players).map(([id, at]) => ({ id, ...at })), rubbings: world.rubbings };
+}
+
+/** Steps with frozen input and state, checking neither changes. */
+class Run {
+  state: IntelState;
+  constructor(
+    readonly config: IntelConfig,
+    seed = 1,
+  ) {
+    this.state = createIntelState(config, seed);
+  }
+
+  step(tick: number, world: World, requests: TargetedRumorRequest[] = []): IntelStepResult {
+    const view = deepFreeze(viewOf(tick, world));
+    const before = hashState(deepFreeze(this.state));
+    const stepped = stepIntel(this.config, this.state, view, deepFreeze(requests));
+    expect(hashState(this.state)).toBe(before);
+    this.state = stepped.state;
+    return stepped;
+  }
+
+  available(tick: number, world: World, playerId: string, type: RubbingType) {
+    return targetedRumorAvailability(this.config, this.state, viewOf(tick, world), playerId, type);
+  }
+}
+
+function to(result: IntelStepResult, playerId: string): IntelMessageBody[] {
+  return result.messages.filter((message) => message.to.kind === "player" && message.to.playerId === playerId).map((message) => message.body);

+
+function everyone(result: IntelStepResult): IntelMessageBody[] {
+  return result.messages.filter((message) => message.to.kind === "everyone").map((message) => message.body);
+}
+
+function only<K extends IntelMessageBody["kind"]>(bodies: IntelMessageBody[], kind: K): Extract<IntelMessageBody, { kind: K }> {

+  expect(found).toHaveLength(1);
+  return found[0] as Extract<IntelMessageBody, { kind: K }>;

+
+const request = (requestId: string, playerId: string, type: RubbingType): TargetedRumorRequest => ({ requestId, playerId, type });
+

+  it("say nothing before control start, then give each player a rumor toward a type they lack", () => {

+  it("give the same rumor for the same seed, and a seed decides between equal targets", () => {

+

57	## 2 Match rules and pacing
58	
59	| Phase | Rule and intended effect |
60	| --- | --- |
61	| Lobby | Public queue or private invitation code; region and connection quality shown |
62	| Ready check | 20 seconds after all eight seats are filled; clients preload arenas |
63	| Departure | 45 seconds of protection; players can explore and collect starter loot |
64	| Exploration | All 12 initial rubbing sources are available; no time gate on collection |
65	| First full set | Final-island sector announced; eligible player receives exact navigation |
66	| Minute 20 | Reveal sectors containing unclaimed rubbings and abandoned rubbing caches |
67	| Minute 28 | Publish approximate sectors of rubbing carriers every 30 seconds |
68	| Minute 35 | Stop the match; if nobody claimed the treasure, record no winner |
69	
70	The match timer begins when player control starts. Eight-player public matches do not start short-handed in version one. Private tests may start with two to eight players and are marked as custom matches. Late arrivals wait in the lobby for another match; they cannot enter an ongoing race.
71	
72	### Spawn fairness
73	
74	Select one of eight prevalidated outer-world spawn slots for each player. Randomize player assignment, island variants, and loot sockets within constraints. Give every player a ship, the same base fighting kit, 50 gold, and a rumor leading toward a reachable objective. Spawn protection permits starter loot and sailing, but collecting a rubbing or initiating a duel ends it immediately.
75	
76	Every slot must offer an initial useful pickup within 20–40 seconds and a plausible rubbing route within 90–150 seconds. Adjacent starting ships must not be in engagement range. These are travel-time targets to validate in playtests, not fixed guarantees based only on map distance.
77	
78	### Time limits and results
79	
80	There is no automatic win for having the most clues at the deadline. A timeout is a draw for victory purposes; the result screen still shows exploration and duel accomplishments. If draws are common, revise travel times and information availability before adding a different scoring system.
81	
82	If a claim completes on the exact deadline tick, process an already-valid completed claim before the timeout. A duel still running at the deadline ends without theft. No match timer is paused for duels, loading, or individual disconnections.
83	
84	## 3 The sea and islands
85	
86	Use a top-down tile world with a fixed navigable layout and authored island templates. Randomize their contents and approved placements. Avoid unrestricted procedural geography in the first release: travel fairness and recognizable landmarks are more valuable than unlimited map variation.
87	
88	| Element | Initial content and behavior |
89	| --- | --- |
90	| Sea | Connected routes, shoals as obstacles, clear docking areas |
91	| Islands | 12 islands drawn from tropical, volcanic, ruin, and mist themes |
92	| Final island | One of several validated hidden sockets; reachable by every ship |
93	| Ruins | One globally claimable rubbing source on each regular island |
94	| Other loot | Fruit pedestals, supply chests, rumor signs, and gold caches |
95	| Landmarks | Visible silhouettes that help players navigate without opening a map |
96	| Hazards | Clearly marked slow zones; no lethal environmental traps in version one |
97	
98	### Movement and visibility
99	
100	Sailing uses acceleration, braking, and turning, with generous handling rather than a naval simulation. Nearby ships and islands are visible inside a defined sight radius. Unvisited territory is covered by fog on the minimap. Once discovered, terrain stays on the personal map, while enemies disappear outside current visibility.
101	
102	World positions are authoritative on the server. Island discovery, enemy visibility, and rumors are evaluated there. The client receives only the hidden-state information it is entitled to know. Public terrain can be shared; objective locations and the final-island choice must not be recoverable from a public random seed.
103	
104	### Exploration activities
105	
106	Each ruin uses one of two short interactions: a three-symbol sequence or a small navigation puzzle. Reading nearby clues solves it; no external One Piece knowledge is required. Completing it permits a six-second rubbing interaction that can be interrupted by a valid encounter. Total time at a fresh ruin should be about 20–40 seconds.
107	
108	Rumors identify an island or sector containing a type the player lacks. Stale rumors are visibly marked after their target is claimed. The journal offers a replacement lead from remaining sources or a coarse carrier sighting. It never guarantees that the destination will remain uncontested.
109	
110	Target neighboring-island travel at 20–40 seconds and the longest useful crossing at 90 seconds or less. Tune map size around those times. Remove empty stretches before adding more sailing mechanics.
111	
112	## 4 Poneglyph ownership and theft
113	
114	Poneglyphs are stationary ancient inscriptions. Players carry their physical rubbings. Use four distinct symbols: Sun, Moon, Tide, and Storm. The match contains three individually identified rubbings of each type, for 12 total. Each of the 12 regular islands begins with one sealed source; assignment is server-controlled.
115	
116	| Rule | Exact behavior |
117	| --- | --- |
118	| Collection | Hold interact for six uninterrupted seconds at an unlocked source |
119	| Inventory | At most one rubbing of each type per player |
120	| Duplicates | Cannot collect or steal a type already held; it stays with its owner |
121	| Completion | Holding all four types enables final navigation and claiming |
122	| Normal defeat | Winner chooses one loser-held type that the winner lacks |
123	| Theft deadline | Five-second choice; default to the eligible type with fewest free sources, then fixed type order |
124	| No eligible type | No rubbing transfers; the gold reward still applies |
125	| Draw | Neither player loses rubbings or gold |
126	| Dropping or trading | Players cannot voluntarily drop, trade, copy, or destroy rubbings |
127	
128	Each rubbing has exactly one location: sealed at a source, owned by a player, held in a recovery cache, or reserved inside an unresolved duel transaction. Its unique ID persists through every transfer. There is no new rubbing spawn when a player loses.
129	
130	### Why multiple copies and limited theft
131	
132	A single global copy of each type would let one player or an abandoned session block the whole match. Three copies allow competing routes to victory. Limiting theft to one type preserves tension without turning a single mistake into a full reset. Players cannot hoard duplicates to remove every route for everyone else.
133	
134	This is a proposed tradeoff: the match has less total-loot brutality than an elimination game, but more opportunities for recovery and rivalry. Measure whether exploration alone is too fast before reducing the supply.
135	
136	### Transfer invariants
137	
138	Commit a duel result and its inventory changes together, once, on the authoritative match process. A repeated result message must not repeat a transfer. Validate winner eligibility again at commit time. The 12 rubbing IDs must remain accounted for until the match ends, including when a player quits during resolution.
139	
140	## 5 Finding and claiming the final treasure
141	
142	When a player first holds all four types, their compass reveals the final island’s exact route. The match announces that a complete set exists and reveals the island’s broad sea sector to everyone. All ships may travel there; four rubbings are required to claim the treasure, not to physically enter the island.
143	
144	This creates a final interception opportunity without requiring every challenger to have completed their own collection. A challenger with fewer than four can stop a leader through a duel, but cannot win until they complete their own set.
145	
146	### Claim sequence
147	
148	1. Reach the treasure circle while holding all four rubbing types.
149	1. End any protection state, stop moving, and hold interact for ten seconds.
150	1. Remain connected, eligible, and free of an accepted duel reservation for the entire channel.
151	1. On completion, the server commits the winner and freezes all match outcomes.
152	
153	Only one claim channel can be active at a time. A second eligible player must interrupt through a valid challenge or wait. Characters do not body-block one another in the overworld. Moving, losing eligibility, disconnecting, or entering a duel resets claim progress to zero.
154	
155	### Counterplay and information
156	
157	Anyone in engagement range can interrupt a claim by successfully starting a duel. The claim UI shows this risk explicitly. Duels remain 1v1: surrounding players cannot damage the fighters or join halfway through. After a duel, the winner receives eight seconds to move away; objective interactions end that protection.
158	
159	Losing a rubbing removes claim eligibility immediately. The game cannot make a person forget a destination they have already learned; the server simply refuses an ineligible claim. Final navigation becomes inactive until the set is restored.
160	
161	### Resolving simultaneous actions
162	
163	On each world tick, process accepted encounter reservations before advancing claim channels. If several attackers qualify in the same tick, choose the closest, then the lowest stable player ID. If several players begin claiming on the same tick, use the same distance-and-ID rule. Inputs arriving after a resolved win cannot retroactively cancel it.
164	
165	The ten-second channel is a deliberate addition to the original “arrive and win” idea. Test both versions. Keep the channel only if it creates exciting finishes without repeated, frustrating stalls.
166

Target neighboring-island travel at 20–40 seconds and the longest useful crossing at 90 seconds or less. Tune map size around those times. Remove empty stretches before adding more sailing mechanics.

## 4 Poneglyph ownership and theft

Poneglyphs are stationary ancient inscriptions. Players carry their physical rubbings. Use four distinct symbols: Sun, Moon, Tide, and Storm. The match contains three individually identified rubbings of each type, for 12 total. Each of the 12 regular islands begins with one sealed source; assignment is server-controlled.

| Rule | Exact behavior |
| --- | --- |
| Collection | Hold interact for six uninterrupted seconds at an unlocked source |
| Inventory | At most one rubbing of each type per player |
| Duplicates | Cannot collect or steal a type already held; it stays with its owner |
| Completion | Holding all four types enables final navigation and claiming |
| Normal defeat | Winner chooses one loser-held type that the winner lacks |
| Theft deadline | Five-second choice; default to the eligible type with fewest free sources, then fixed type order |
| No eligible type | No rubbing transfers; the gold reward still applies |
| Draw | Neither player loses rubbings or gold |
| Dropping or trading | Players cannot voluntarily drop, trade, copy, or destroy rubbings |

Each rubbing has exactly one location: sealed at a source, owned by a player, held in a recovery cache, or reserved inside an unresolved duel transaction. Its unique ID persists through every transfer. There is no new rubbing spawn when a player loses.

### Why multiple copies and limited theft

A single global copy of each type would let one player or an abandoned session block the whole match. Three copies allow competing routes to victory. Limiting theft to one type preserves tension without turning a single mistake into a full reset. Players cannot hoard duplicates to remove every route for everyone else.

This is a proposed tradeoff: the match has less total-loot brutality than an elimination game, but more opportunities for recovery and rivalry. Measure whether exploration alone is too fast before reducing the supply.

### Transfer invariants

Commit a duel result and its inventory changes together, once, on the authoritative match process. A repeated result message must not repeat a transfer. Validate winner eligibility again at commit time. The 12 rubbing IDs must remain accounted for until the match ends, including when a player quits during resolution.

## 5 Finding and claiming the final treasure

When a player first holds all four types, their compass reveals the final island’s exact route. The match announces that a complete set exists and reveals the island’s broad sea sector to everyone. All ships may travel there; four rubbings are required to claim the treasure, not to physically enter the island.

This creates a final interception opportunity without requiring every challenger to have completed their own collection. A challenger with fewer than four can stop a leader through a duel, but cannot win until they complete their own set.

### Claim sequence

1. Reach the treasure circle while holding all four rubbing types.
1. End any protection state, stop moving, and hold interact for ten seconds.
1. Remain connected, eligible, and free of an accepted duel reservation for the entire channel.
1. On completion, the server commits the winner and freezes all match outcomes.

Only one claim channel can be active at a time. A second eligible player must interrupt through a valid challenge or wait. Characters do not body-block one another in the overworld. Moving, losing eligibility, disconnecting, or entering a duel resets claim progress to zero.

### Counterplay and information

Anyone in engagement range can interrupt a claim by successfully starting a duel. The claim UI shows this risk explicitly. Duels remain 1v1: surrounding players cannot damage the fighters or join halfway through. After a duel, the winner receives eight seconds to move away; objective interactions end that protection.

Losing a rubbing removes claim eligibility immediately. The game cannot make a person forget a destination they have already learned; the server simply refuses an ineligible claim. Final navigation becomes inactive until the set is restored.

### Resolving simultaneous actions

On each world tick, process accepted encounter reservations before advancing claim channels. If several attackers qualify in the same tick, choose the closest, then the lowest stable player ID. If several players begin claiming on the same tick, use the same distance-and-ID rule. Inputs arriving after a resolved win cannot retroactively cancel it.

The ten-second channel is a deliberate addition to the original “arrive and win” idea. Test both versions. Keep the channel only if it creates exciting finishes without repeated, frustrating stalls.
